reference_answer:
The question's opening summarizes a named theorem but is not a complete hypothesis list for unrestricted algebraic representations. Linearity of an ENDOMORPHISM is essential, and the standard scalar conclusion is guaranteed for a FINITE-DIMENSIONAL representation over an algebraically closed base. Algebraic closure alone does not guarantee scalarity in arbitrary algebraic dimension. These are part of the requested boundary assessment, not new standing assumptions placed on every representation in the question.

The genuinely general surviving statement is this. Let F be any field, let G be any group, and let V,W be NONZERO algebraically irreducible F-linear representations, with no finite-dimension, topology, finiteness or characteristic restriction. If f:V->W is F-linear and intertwines the actions, ker f and im f are invariant LINEAR subspaces: f(rho_V(g)v)=rho_W(g)f(v) preserves zero, and rho_W(g)f(v)=f(rho_V(g)v) lies in the image. If f!=0, its kernel is not V and its image is not0. Algebraic irreducibility gives ker f=0 and im f=W, so f is bijective. Its inverse is F-linear and is also an intertwiner: the equality f rho_V(g)=rho_W(g) f can be multiplied by f^-1 on both sides. No rank-nullity argument or finite-dimensional surjectivity shortcut is needed.

Consequently D=End_G(V), consisting of F-LINEAR commuting endomorphisms, is a division ring for nonzero V. It is closed under addition, multiplication by composition and additive inverses; the identity is nonzero, and every nonzero element has its inverse inside D by the preceding calculation. Scalars lambda I form a central copy of F. This conclusion does not assert that D is commutative or equal to F. For finite-dimensional V, D is also a finite-dimensional F-algebra because it is an F-linear subspace of End_F(V), of dimension at most(dim_F V)². That finite-dimensional algebra conclusion must not be silently carried over to arbitrary V.

Here is the requested genuine real counterexample. Let G=C4 be generated by g and act on V=R² by J=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. Since J²=-I and J4=I, this defines a representation. A proper nonzero real invariant subspace would be a line Rv, so Jv=a v for real a; applying J again would give-v=a²v, impossible for v!=0. Thus the action is irreducible over R. It is not merely an arbitrary rotation: an identity or half-turn would not prove this irreducibility.

For A=[[p,q],[r,s]], the relation AJ=JA reads [[q,-p],[s,-r]]=[[-r,-s],[p,q]], so p=s and r=-q. Equivalently the full commutant is D={aI+bJ:a,b in R}, with matrices[[a,-b],[b,a]]. The map a+i b -> aI+bJ is a bijective real-algebra homomorphism, because J²=-I, so D is isomorphic to C and strictly contains RI. J itself is a nonscalar commuting endomorphism. Every nonzero aI+bJ has determinant a²+b²>0 and inverse(aI-bJ)/(a²+b²), verifying the division property directly. No real eigenvalue for J is exactly the missing eigenvalue step in the scalar proof. Complexifying this same two-space produces the eigenlines for plus/minus i, so it is not a complex irreducible counterexample.

The correct scalar corollary is conditional, not 'scalar iff the field is algebraically closed'. For a nonzero finite-dimensional algebraically irreducible representation over an algebraically closed F, every f in D has a nonconstant characteristic polynomial with a root lambda in F. Hence ker(f-lambda I) contains a nonzero eigenvector. Since f-lambda I is still an intertwiner, part(i) says it is zero or invertible; the nonzero kernel excludes invertibility, giving f=lambda I. Thus D=F I in this finite-dimensional setting. No finite group, group-order division or characteristic-zero assumption is used. For a particular possibly infinite-dimensional V it is already sufficient that every f in D have a base-field eigenvalue, or more generally that every f be algebraic over an algebraically closed F: a split annihilating polynomial is a product of f-lambda I factors, and a division ring has no zero divisors, so one factor vanishes. Finite dimension is a convenient uniform sufficient condition, not a necessary condition for scalarity in every individual representation. A real one-dimensional character, for example, already has D=R even though R is not algebraically closed.

To refute unrestricted collapse rather than merely warn about it, put K=C(t), G=K^times and V=K as a complex vector space, with action by multiplication. This is a complex-linear group representation. The independent powers1,t,t²,... show infinite dimension. If an invariant complex subspace contains w!=0, multiplication by v/w carries it to any v!=0, so the action is genuinely algebraically irreducible. Its FULL commutant is K: if f commutes with every multiplication by g!=0, then for v!=0, f(v)=f(v*1)=v f(1), while linearity handles0. Conversely every multiplication M_a commutes with the action. Thus f=M_a and a->M_a identifies End_G(V) with K, a division field strictly larger than C. M_t is nonscalar, and M_t-lambda I is invertible via multiplication by1/(t-lambda) for every complex lambda, so it has no complex eigenvalue. Algebraic closure alone therefore cannot collapse this infinite-dimensional division ring. Replacing C by R yields the same construction with full commutant R(t), an infinite-dimensional real division field; an unrestricted R/C/H-only classification is false. The separate classification of finite-dimensional associative real division algebras is not needed, proved or claimed here.

If a convention admits V0 as irreducible by a vacuous invariant-subspace predicate, End_G(0) is the zero ring, not a nontrivial division ring containing an injected copy of F. Its only map0 is of course a scalar multiple of the zero identity; scalar uniqueness and nonzero eigenvector arguments are not claimed there. All division-ring assertions above explicitly concern nonzero V. Finally, these are algebraic statements about all invariant linear subspaces. In a Hilbert-space variant with only CLOSED invariant subspaces and bounded operators, an algebraic image could be dense rather than surjective, so the kernel/image proof alone would not establish the same conclusion. Continuous/unitary operator-Schur variants require separate topological/functional-analytic hypotheses and proofs. No topology, completeness, boundedness or quantum resource bound is manufactured for C(t), and no such Hilbert theorem is established or refuted here.

exposition.core_summary: Linear Schur(i) gives a division ring for any nonzero algebraically irreducible representation, without finite dimension. A real C4 plane has full commutant C. Finite dimension plus algebraic closure forces scalars; closure alone fails on C(t), and neither condition is an iff criterion for individual scalar commutants.

semantic_steps.claim: Over any field and algebraic dimension, linear intertwiners between nonzero irreps are zero or isomorphisms; scalar Schur additionally has an eigenvalue hypothesis, uniformly supplied by finite dimension plus algebraic closure.
The C4 generator J=[[0,-1],[1,0]] acts irreducibly on R², since a real invariant line would imply a²=-1.
Solving AJ=JA gives exactly{aI+bJ}, isomorphic to C and strictly larger than RI; every nonzero element has inverse(aI-bJ)/(a²+b²).

The general nonzero-irrep commutant is a division ring, not automatically scalars or finite-dimensional. The conditional scalar theorem, C(t) infinite counterexample, zero ring and algebraic-versus-closed-subspace boundaries are explicit.
